Monday. In Bhavna's Class 10, the new teacher praised Sonali three times for her "beautiful English." When Ganesh answered a history question in Marathi-flavoured English, the teacher said, "Try again, properly." Ganesh's answer had been right. Bhavna noticed, and felt uneasy.
Wednesday. At lunch, Sonali imitated Ganesh's accent. Bhavna laughed along before she could stop herself. Then she saw Ganesh's face and felt her stomach drop.
Friday. In the group project, Ganesh explained the whole Maratha chapter to them in Marathi, fast and brilliant, better than any of them. Bhavna said, "Ganesh, you should present this part. In English or Marathi, whichever." Sonali rolled her eyes. Ganesh looked surprised, then nodded.
Walking home, Bhavna thought: speaking English well had never meant knowing more. She was annoyed that she'd believed it.

qa.a: The teacher praised Sonali three times for her "beautiful English."

qa.q: What was Bhavna feeling when she saw Ganesh's face at lunch?
qa.a: Bhavna felt guilty and ashamed, her stomach dropping, after laughing along at the imitation.

qa.q: Which choice did Bhavna make on Friday, and why was it fair?
qa.a: She asked Ganesh to present the part he knew best in whichever language he liked, valuing his knowledge over his accent.

qa.q: How might Ganesh feel when the teacher says "Try again, properly"?
qa.a: Ganesh probably felt humiliated and discouraged, since his answer was right but was treated as lesser because of his English.

subtopic: Language identity, Hinglish, regional pride and code-switching

Dhruv, you're mocking the new boy's English? Let your Payal Dadi tell you about a girl named Kamala.
I was sixteen, at a convent school in Allahabad. English was everything there. The girls who spoke it smoothly were made monitors and sent to welcome guests. Kamala came from a Hindi-medium school. When she read aloud, the nuns corrected every word, and we giggled.
I giggled too. Then we had a Hindi poetry recitation, and Kamala recited Mahadevi Verma so beautifully that the whole hall went silent. Afterwards I heard one of the nuns say, "Pity her English is so weak."
That sentence stayed with me. I thought: she's cleverer than all of us, and they only hear her accent. I started sitting with Kamala at lunch. She taught me Hindi poetry; I helped with her English.
So, Dhruv, the language someone speaks is not the size of their mind.

qa.q: Whose poetry did Kamala recite?
qa.a: Kamala recited Mahadevi Verma.

qa.q: How did Payal feel when she heard the nun's remark?
qa.a: Payal felt uncomfortable and troubled, realising that Kamala was cleverer than all of them but was judged only by her accent.

qa.q: What was the turning point inside Payal's story?
qa.a: Hearing the nun say "Pity her English is so weak" after Kamala's recitation made Payal see the bias, and she began sitting with Kamala at lunch.

qa.q: What might Kamala have felt when the girls giggled at her reading?
qa.a: Kamala probably felt embarrassed and lonely, treated as lesser in a school where English was everything.

grounding: An elder recalls noticing as a teenager that fluent English earned respect while a Hindi-medium classmate was undervalued, and choosing to resist that bias.

subtopic: Language identity, Hinglish, regional pride and code-switching
passage:
The inter-school quiz had thirty seconds per question, and the quizmaster only accepted answers in English. Abhinav, sixteen, sat at the buzzer beside his teammate Rafiq, who'd grown up speaking Urdu at home.
"Which river is called the Sorrow of Bihar?"
Rafiq whispered, "Kosi!" but then fumbled the English sentence. The buzzer on the other team went, and they got the points.
In the break, a boy from the other school laughed. "Your partner can't even speak English."
Abhinav felt his face go hot. He'd laughed at jokes like that before. Not now.
"He knew every answer in this round," Abhinav said. "Knowing and speaking English aren't the same thing."
He turned to Rafiq. "You answer, I'll say it in English. Just tell me fast."
For the next round, Rafiq whispered answers and Abhinav spoke them. They won by ten points.

qa.q: How many seconds did each question get?
qa.a: The inter-school quiz had thirty seconds per question.

qa.q: What was Abhinav feeling when the boy laughed at Rafiq?
qa.a: Abhinav felt angry and a little ashamed, remembering that he had laughed at jokes like that before.

qa.q: What did Abhinav's plan show about language and intelligence?
qa.a: By letting Rafiq supply the answers while he spoke them in English, Abhinav showed that Rafiq's knowledge was never the problem, only the language rule.

qa.q: How might Rafiq feel after they win?
qa.a: Rafiq would likely feel proud and relieved, his knowledge finally counted rather than judged by his English.

grounding: Under quiz pressure, a teenager notices that English fluency is mistaken for intelligence and resists the bias by standing with his teammate.

First week. Manoj, nineteen, a fierce lover of Kannada, fumed at the new English-and-Hindi-only signboard in the college canteen. "In our own state!" he said loudly to his roommate Eshaan, from Lucknow. Then he added, "Hindi people come here and expect everyone to adjust." Eshaan went quiet.
Third week. Eshaan asked Manoj to teach him Kannada numbers so he could buy vegetables. Manoj taught him, grinning at his mistakes. That night Manoj felt a twinge: he'd said "Hindi people" as if Eshaan were a problem.

Nilesh, you've been shouting on the internet about people who don't speak Marathi? Let your old Manoj Kaka tell you something.
In 1998, I was twenty, a student in Pune, and I was angry. Offices were putting up English-only forms; shopkeepers answered me in Hindi in my own city. I joined a group that marched for Marathi. Good. I loved my language, I still do.
But one evening in the group, some boys talked about "teaching a lesson" to a Tamil student who ran a small canteen near college. I felt sick. That student, Murugan, had fed me on credit for three months when my father was ill.
I left the group that night. I went to Murugan's canteen and ate there, loudly speaking Marathi, and he answered me in his broken Marathi, and we laughed.
Pride, Nilesh, is loving your own. Contempt is hating someone else's. Keep the first.

subtopic: Language identity, Hinglish, regional pride and code-switching

The college fest's debate on "One Nation, One Language" started in fifteen minutes, and Ujjwal, twenty, still hadn't finished his speech. He was arguing against it, with every ounce of his love for Bangla. His draft ended with a line mocking Hindi as "a language without poetry."
His teammate Francis, from Goa, read it over his shoulder. "Ujjwal, you're arguing for Bangla. Why insult Hindi?"
"Because they're forcing it on us."
"Some people are. The language isn't. My mother reads Hindi poems to me. Konkani too."
Ujjwal stared at the line. The bell rang for the first speaker.
He crossed the line out and wrote: "Every language, Hindi included, carries someone's grandmother's lullaby. That's why none should be forced."
On stage, that line got the loudest applause. Francis gave him a thumbs-up from the wings.

qa.a: Francis is from Goa.

qa.q: What was Ujjwal feeling when Francis questioned his draft?
qa.a: Ujjwal felt defensive and proud, angry that Hindi was being forced, and then uncertain as he stared at his own insult.

qa.q: What made Ujjwal's final line stronger?
qa.a: It kept his love for Bangla and his argument against forcing a language, but without contempt, which respected every language.

qa.q: How might Francis see the argument about languages?
qa.a: Francis sees that a language itself isn't the enemy, since his mother reads both Hindi and Konkani poems to him.

grounding: Under time pressure before a debate, a young adult's pride in Bangla nearly turns into contempt for Hindi, and a friend helps him keep pride without scorn.

subtopic: Language identity, Hinglish, regional pride and code-switching
passage:
In the small grocery near his dorm in Leipzig, Omar, nineteen, pointed at a loaf of bread and said, "This, please." The cashier replied in rapid German. Omar understood nothing. A queue formed behind him. Someone sighed loudly. His face burned; he left without the bread.
That evening, his landlady, Fatima, a Turkish-German woman who had moved here thirty years ago, knocked with soup. "You look like I did in my first month," she said.
She wrote five phrases on a card: please, thank you, I don't understand, slower please, how much. "Say them badly. People soften when you try."
The next morning, Omar went back to the grocery. "Langsamer, bitte," he said, blushing. The cashier smiled for the first time and repeated the price slowly, pointing at the screen.
He walked out with the bread, and a strange small pride.

qa.q: How many phrases did Fatima write on the card?
qa.a: She wrote five phrases on a card.

qa.q: What was Omar feeling when he left without the bread?
qa.a: Omar felt embarrassed and like an outsider, his face burning as the queue grew and someone sighed.

qa.q: Why did Fatima's advice work?
qa.a: Learning a few basic phrases and trying them, even badly, showed effort, and the cashier responded by slowing down.

qa.q: How might the cashier see Omar differently the next morning?
qa.a: When Omar tried a German phrase, the cashier may have seen a newcomer making an effort, which made her patient and friendly.

grounding: Outside India, a student in a new city struggles at a shop, feels an outsider, and wins goodwill by learning basic phrases while a local slows down.

subtopic: Language identity, Hinglish, regional pride and code-switching

In the first week at her college in Chennai, Anjali, eighteen, from Patna, understood about half of each lecture. The professors switched into Tamil to explain jokes and examples. Classmates laughed, and she laughed a second late. At the canteen, she pointed at dishes because she couldn't pronounce them.
One afternoon, the professor asked her a question in Tamil by mistake. The room waited. Anjali froze.
Ira, from the next bench, whispered the question in English. Anjali answered, correctly.
After class, Ira said, "I'll teach you ten words a day. And tell the others to slow down around you."
"Why are you helping me?"
"Because my cousin went to Delhi and nobody helped her."
By the end of the month, Anjali could order curd rice properly and say "konjam mella" (a little slower), which made even the canteen uncle grin.

Dear Simran,
Three weeks in Pune now. You asked how it's going. Honestly? I feel like a deaf person some days.
At the vegetable market, the woman speaks Marathi so fast. I say "Kitna?" and she answers in Marathi and I just hand her a note and hope. In the hostel, the boys joke in Marathi and I laugh a second late.
But something good happened yesterday. The watchman, Shinde Kaka, stopped me at the gate and said slowly, "Wasim, you learn one Marathi word each day, I teach." Today's word was "kiti," how much. I used it at the market. The vegetable woman laughed, then slowed right down and counted on her fingers.
I felt like a small child learning to walk. But a happy one.
Next time I'll tell you "dhanyavaad" in Marathi. Wish me luck.
Wasim

subtopic: Language identity, Hinglish, regional pride and code-switching

Varun, you told me today you feel "fake" in client meetings. Let Eshaan Sir tell you something from twenty years ago.
I was twenty-four, my first job at a bank in Mumbai. At home in Kanpur we spoke Awadhi-Hindi. In the office, everyone spoke polished English, and I practised mine in the mirror every night.
One day, my manager heard me on the phone with my mother, speaking Awadhi. I blushed. He said, "Two languages, two tools. Don't throw either away."
I thought about that. After that, I stopped apologising for my accent. At client meetings, I used my best English. At lunch with the peons and drivers, I spoke Hindi. With my mother, Awadhi. I felt whole, not fake, because I never pretended the other parts didn't exist.
So, Varun, use your English for the clients. And call your grandmother in Bhojpuri tonight.

qa.q: What did Eshaan practise in the mirror every night?
qa.a: He practised his English in the mirror every night.

qa.q: What was Eshaan feeling when the manager heard him speak Awadhi?
qa.a: Eshaan felt embarrassed, blushing at being overheard speaking his home language.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Eshaan's story?
qa.a: The manager's words about two languages being two tools helped Eshaan stop apologising and use each language where it fit.

qa.q: How might Eshaan's mother have felt hearing him keep Awadhi?
qa.a: She would probably feel close to him and reassured that city life hadn't taken away their shared language.

The client call from Singapore was starting in three minutes, and Keerthana's phone buzzed. Amma. She picked up.
"Kanna, did you eat? Appa's medicine came?" in fast Tamil.
"Saaptaen, Amma. I'll call after the meeting, okay?" Keerthana answered, laughing, in the same Tamil.
Sachin, her teammate, was setting up the screen. When she hung up, he grinned. "Two minutes later you'll sound like a newsreader."
The call began. Keerthana, twenty-five, switched into crisp, polished English, walking the client through the numbers without a single slip.
Afterwards, Sachin said, "Doesn't it feel weird? Like two people?"
Keerthana thought about it. "No. It's one person with two toolkits. Tamil is where I rest. English is where I work." She picked up her phone. "Now I'm calling Amma back."

In the open-plan office in Andheri, Shreya, twenty-four, had just finished presenting to the regional heads in careful, polished English. Her colleague Pranav leaned over. "Where did that accent come from? At lunch you sound like a Dadar fish market."
A few people laughed. Shreya felt a flicker of irritation, then let it go.
"At lunch I speak Marathi, because that's who I am," she said. "In meetings I speak English, because that's my job. Both are me."
Pranav raised his eyebrows. "Isn't it tiring?"
"Less tiring than pretending I'm only one of them."
That evening, on the local train, she called her Aai in Marathi and laughed about the presentation. Then she replied to a work email in English, and switched back again mid-sentence to tell Aai about the dinner she wanted.

Dear Diary,
Second week at the school in Dehradun. Everyone here has shiny black shoes. Mine are the old brown ones from our village near Leh. Today a boy asked if I'd walked here on a yak. Everyone laughed. I laughed too so they wouldn't see my face.
I also didn't know what "canteen coupon" meant, so I didn't eat.
But then Ankita, who sits next to me, gave me half her paratha. She showed me how the coupons work. She said, "My Nani's village doesn't even have a road. You're not behind. You just came from far."
Ma'am asked me to tell the class about apricot season. I told them how we dry apricots on the roof. They asked so many questions!
Maybe tomorrow I'll be less scared.
Tenzin

Arohi, ten, from our Bengaluru batch, has been the happiest child on this trip. She runs barefoot in the fields and told me today, "I want to live here forever. No traffic, no homework!"

She came back quiet. "Pooja does this every day before school," she told me. "And she still has homework."
